vignette:
He is 30, a single African man who works as a curriculum designer, and he talks about the relationship as if it began in two different worlds. In the first world, his former partner is charming, funny, attentive to detail, the kind of person who remembers how he takes his tea and sends messages in the middle of the day asking whether he has eaten. In the second world, which reveals itself slowly and then all at once, she watches him constantly, checks his phone, mocks his work, and turns ordinary disagreements into interrogations that leave him apologizing for things he does not understand.

At first, he tells himself that the tension is stress. He is deep into a demanding project, building learning materials and sequencing content for a new school program, spending long hours refining objectives and assessments. He prides himself on precision. He likes order, progression, the feeling that ideas can be shaped into something useful. At home, though, order stops helping him. If he comes back later than expected, she accuses him of hiding something. If he is quiet, she says he is disrespecting her. When she grabs his wrist during an argument for the first time, hard enough to leave finger-shaped marks, he is more shocked than afraid. He remembers staring at his skin and thinking how strange it is that evidence can appear so quickly.

The abuse becomes physical in ways that are sudden and disorienting. She shoves him into a wall during an argument about a message from a female colleague. Another time she throws a ceramic mug that narrowly misses his face and shatters near the kitchen doorway. The worst incident happens late at night after he says he wants to spend the weekend alone to finish a curriculum review. She blocks the door, slaps him repeatedly, and when he tries to move past her she punches him in the side of the head. He falls against a table and feels, more than hears, the impact. What he remembers most clearly is not pain but confusion: the bright living room light, the ringing in his ears, her voice suddenly sounding far away. Afterward she cries, says he made her do it, then says she cannot live without him. He helps pick up the broken things with shaking hands.

He does not tell anyone for a long time. Part of him is ashamed that he stays. Part of him thinks no one will take seriously that a man is being hurt by his partner. He becomes careful in the relationship in the way one becomes careful around a faulty wire-watching for sparks, planning routes through each day. He speaks softly, offers quick reassurance, avoids topics that might trigger anger. At work, where he is usually known for thoughtful collaboration, he begins to lose his place in meetings. A colleague asks a simple question about a learning sequence he designed, and he realizes he has not heard the last minute of conversation. His body is in the conference room, but his mind is fixed on whether there will be another accusation waiting on his phone.

After he finally leaves, the danger does not feel over. He changes locks, blocks numbers, and still startles when footsteps pause outside his apartment door. He sleeps badly. Sometimes he jerks awake with his heart pounding, certain for a few seconds that she is in the room. He avoids the street near her old building even when it makes his commute longer. If he hears raised voices in public, his chest tightens and his vision narrows. Once, in a grocery store, a couple begins arguing near the checkout line and he abandons his basket and walks out into the parking lot, sweating through his shirt.

He tells me that what disturbs him most is how his mind keeps returning to moments he does not invite. While editing lesson materials, he will suddenly see the mug exploding by the doorway or feel again the blow to the side of his head. He tries to push the images away by working harder, polishing language, reorganizing units, checking formatting long after the task is finished. He has become someone who rereads emails five times before sending them. He sits with his back to the wall in cafés. He scans rooms automatically. He says he is tired of feeling as if his nervous system learned a lesson his thinking mind cannot unteach.

He used to enjoy designing curriculum because it meant imagining growth-how people build understanding step by step. Now concentration comes in short bursts. He opens a document and stares at the screen, then notices he has been listening for sounds in the hallway. Friends invite him out and he often declines, saying he is busy. The truth is that being around people feels effortful; he mistrusts his own judgment and worries about questions he does not want to answer. He speaks about himself more cautiously now, as if disclosure itself has become dangerous.

Even so, there are glimpses of the person he recognizes. He describes the satisfaction of seeing a well-structured module come together, the pleasure of making something clear and teachable. He has begun calling his sister more often. Some mornings he notices that he has slept through the night and feels almost surprised. But the past remains close. He is still living with the afterimage of violence, measuring ordinary moments against the possibility that harm can arrive inside intimacy and call itself love.
